newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels fired warning shots, Red Cross says.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels fired warning shots, Red Cross says.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 74 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home in Peru fired four shots in the air during the night, making their heavily armed presence felt as officials tried to restart negotiations on Friday.
Red Cross officials said the hostages were calm and no one was injured by the shots fired by Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels who stormed the residence 24 days ago.

"No one was injured and according to the MRTA they were warning shots into the air," International Committee of the Red Cross spokeswoman Cecilia Baux told Reuters. "The situation is calm and the flow of food and messages is normal."
She did not say why the rebels felt the need to fire the shots. A police officer on duty close to the site said: "They're reminding us that they are still in there."

Chief Red Cross representative Michel Minnig, who has been the main channel of contact between the rebels and the outside world, entered the residence twice on Friday but there was no sign of any resumption of hostage releases.
The rebels, who stormed a Dec. 17 cocktail party in honour of Japanese Emperor Akihito, are armed with AKM assault rifles and grenades and have booby-trapped and mined the compound.
It was the second time this week that detonations have been heard within the besieged diplomatic residence at night.
Two shots were heard early on Tuesday as a man, presumed to be one of the MRTA rebels, ran across the front part of the compound towards the building.

The guerrillas are using their hostages to pressure Peru's government into releasing about 400 jailed comrades. President Alberto Fujimori has rejected this demand and told the rebels to put down their weapons and free the hostages.
The MRTA originally took more than 500 hostages but have released more than 430. None has been released since New Year's Day when initial contacts between the two sides appeared to break down.
The rebels are still holding top government and security force officials, Japanese businessmen and diplomats and Fujimori's younger brother, Pedro.
In an effort to relaunch contact with the rebels, Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi said on Thursday they may be allowed to leave the country if the crisis ended peacefully.
"In a timely manner, we will announce to the press which countries would be disposed to receive these men," he said.

Fujimori has stuck to his tough line against the rebels, lambasting them as "terrorists" bent on pointless violence, but has said he will not consider storming the residence so long as the hostages are not harmed.
Officials say a "commission of guarantors" may be set up to oversee a peaceful solution to the crisis but have given no details.
Peruvian police on Friday continued to hold a reporter and a translator from Japan's TV Asahi who sneaked into the compound on Tuesday and interviewed rebel leader Nestor Cerpa.
The network's interview has not been seen because police arrested the two men as they left and confiscated their material. TV Asahi has said it wants the videotape shot by the team returned.

The newspaper El Comercio quoted police sources on Friday as saying that the MRTA, which like the larger Shining Path guerrilla movement has been hard hit by Fujimori's drive against rebel groups in recent years, has been reduced to a force of about 230 fighters in the central Peruvian jungle.
Their last known action was an ambush in the Pichanaqui valley, about 217.5 miles (350 km) east of Lima, on Dec. 3 in which one soldier died, it added.
